question: The EU aims to become climate-neutral by 2050, a goal reaffirmed in numerous Commission strategies and legislative packages. A 2021 study estimates that achieving this target will require investments of up to EUR 28 trillion1. This corresponds to nearly EUR 1 trillion per year – a sum that imposes significant burdens on households and businesses.

Given that the EU’s contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions is approximately 6 %2, this raises the question of what impact such investments will have on global temperatures. In the light of the above: 1.
To what extent does the Commission estimate that global average temperatures will be reduced by 2050 if the EU allocates the investments as required under the European Green Deal?
How does the Commission calculate the impact of EU policies on global average temperatures by 2050?

Has the Commission evaluated the extent to which projected emission increases by major economies outside the EU could offset or undermine the temperature reductions achieved through the European green deal?

‘Europe’s path to climate-neutral by 2050 costs roughly EUR 28 trillion’, Consultancy.eu website, 24 August 2021, https://www.consultancy.eu/news/6663/europes-path-to-climate-neutral-by-2050-costs-roughly-28trillion. European Parliament ‘Climate change in Europe: facts and figures’, European Parliament website, 19 July 2018, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/topics/en/article/20180703STO07123/climate-change-in-europe-factsand-figures.
answer: Since the ratification of the Paris Agreement on climate change, commitments by countries around the world have contributed to reducing projected global warming from 3.7 — 4.8°C to 2.4 — 2.6°C (1).

This shows the importance of ambitious leadership and concrete climate action, such as that of the EU and its Member States, to avoid uncontrolled global warming and the damages it brings for economies, ecosystems, well-being, ultimately contributing to political instability (2). The European Climate Law (ECL) and its climate targets ensure that the EU remains a global climate leader.
Investments are necessary regardless of the EU decarbonisation pathway, to replace ageing assets and infrastructure and to respond to growing energy needs.

Delivering on the targets under the ECL provides certainty and boosts such investments in a modern EU energy system, independence, strategic autonomy and enhanced security, while limiting the costs of climate inaction which far outweigh investments needed (3), (4), (5).

The Clean Industrial Deal and Net-Zero Industry Act (6) outline concrete actions to turn decarbonisation into a driver of growth for European (7) industries. Limiting global average temperature is a collective effort, all countries must act to reduce emissions. Climate targets reflect global cost-effective Greenhouse gas pathways aligned with the Paris Agreement temperature goals.
EU climate policy gives credibility to the EU’s calls on others to act and accelerate decarbonisation (8). 1
